tips.title: Choosing the Right Cement for ABS vs Polystyrene
tips.text: Tamiya Extra Thin Cement bonds polystyrene perfectly by melting the plastic together, but it struggles with ABS parts found in many modern kits (breeches, gun barrels, ICM and Arma Hobby aircraft propellers). For ABS, switch to Tamiya ABS & Polystyrene Cement in the green bottle, which contains ABS-compatible solvents. Apply sparingly with a fine brush to both surfaces, press together for 10 seconds, and let cure for 24 hours before sanding. Test the bond on a spare sprue first.

tips.title: Selecting the Correct Paint Type: Acrylic vs Enamel vs Lacquer
tips.text: For most scale model applications, Vallejo Acrylic Paints (Model Air or Model Color) are versatile and user-friendly. They're water-based, non-toxic, and dry quickly. However, if you're aiming for a durable, glossy finish like that on vintage vehicles or aircraft, consider enamels like Tamiya Acrylic Gloss Enamel. Lacquers like Vallejo Lacquer Thinner offer quick drying and excellent adhesion but require a spray booth and proper ventilation.

tips.title: Choosing the Right Sandpaper Grits for Each Stage
tips.text: For pre-shaping and smoothing, use medium grit sandpaper like 220 or 320. For Tamiya, Eduard, and ICM kits, start with 220 to remove mold lines and flash, then progress to 320 for a smoother finish before painting. For finer details and after painting, switch to wet or dry sanding with 500 or 1000 grit. Always sand in one direction and check progress with a magnifying glass.

tips.title: Filling Gaps: Tamiya Putty vs Vallejo Plastic Putty
tips.text: For small gaps and imperfections, Tamiya Putty in the red bottle is ideal. Apply with a brush, let it dry for 20 minutes, then scrape off excess with a scalpel. For larger gaps or uneven surfaces, Vallejo Plastic Putty offers better coverage and self-leveling properties. Apply with a palette knife, let dry for 30 minutes, then scrape and sand. Avoid super glue and baking soda mixtures as they can create bubbles and are difficult to sand.

tips.title: Selecting Photo-Etch vs Resin Detail Parts
tips.text: Photo-etch (PE) parts from Eduard, Eduard's Freight Car Sets, and Arma Hobby offer intricate details but require careful handling and bending. For complex shapes, use bending tools designed for PE, like those by Microscale or Eduard. Resin detail parts, like those from Clear Prop Models, offer high detail and ease of handling but may require some trimming and cleanup. Choose based on your skill level, the complexity of the parts, and whether they're available in your desired scale.
